[258](https://docs.rs#258)/// Comparison of two pointer-like things.
[259](https://docs.rs#259)// A and B are likely to *be* references, or thin wrappers around that. Calling that with extra
[260](https://docs.rs#260)// reference is just annoying.
[261](https://docs.rs#261)#[allow(clippy::needless_pass_by_value)]
[262](https://docs.rs#262)fn ptr_eq<Base, A, B>(a: A, b: B) -> bool
[263](https://docs.rs#263)where
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    A: AsRaw<Base>,
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    B: AsRaw<Base>,
[266](https://docs.rs#266){
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    let a = a.as_raw();
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    let b = b.as_raw();
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    ptr::eq(a, b)
[270](https://docs.rs#270)}
[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)/// An atomic storage for a reference counted smart pointer like [`Arc`] or `Option<Arc>`.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)///
[274](https://docs.rs#274)/// This is a storage where a smart pointer may live. It can be read and written atomically from
[275](https://docs.rs#275)/// several threads, but doesn't act like a pointer itself.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)/// One can be created [`from`] an [`Arc`]. To get the pointer back, use the
[278](https://docs.rs#278)/// [`load`](#method.load).
[279](https://docs.rs#279)///
[280](https://docs.rs#280)/// # Note
[281](https://docs.rs#281)///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)/// This is the common generic implementation. This allows sharing the same code for storing
[283](https://docs.rs#283)/// both `Arc` and `Option<Arc>` (and possibly other similar types).
[284](https://docs.rs#284)///
[285](https://docs.rs#285)/// In your code, you most probably want to interact with it through the
[286](https://docs.rs#286)/// [`ArcSwap`](type.ArcSwap.html) and [`ArcSwapOption`](type.ArcSwapOption.html) aliases. However,
[287](https://docs.rs#287)/// the methods they share are described here and are applicable to both of them. That's why the
[288](https://docs.rs#288)/// examples here use `ArcSwap` ‒ but they could as well be written with `ArcSwapOption` or
[289](https://docs.rs#289)/// `ArcSwapAny`.
[290](https://docs.rs#290)///
[291](https://docs.rs#291)/// # Type parameters
[292](https://docs.rs#292)///
[293](https://docs.rs#293)/// * `T`: The smart pointer to be kept inside. This crate provides implementation for `Arc<_>` and
[294](https://docs.rs#294)///   `Option<Arc<_>>` (`Rc` too, but that one is not practically useful). But third party could
[295](https://docs.rs#295)///   provide implementations of the [`RefCnt`] trait and plug in others.
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// * `S`: Chooses the [strategy] used to protect the data inside. They come with various
[297](https://docs.rs#297)///   performance trade offs, the default [`DefaultStrategy`] is good rule of thumb for most use
[298](https://docs.rs#298)///   cases.
[299](https://docs.rs#299)///
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// # Examples
[301](https://docs.rs#301)///
[302](https://docs.rs#302)/// ```rust
[303](https://docs.rs#303)/// # use std::sync::Arc;
[304](https://docs.rs#304)/// # use arc_swap::ArcSwap;
[305](https://docs.rs#305)/// let arc = Arc::new(42);
[306](https://docs.rs#306)/// let arc_swap = ArcSwap::from(arc);
[307](https://docs.rs#307)/// assert_eq!(42, **arc_swap.load());
[308](https://docs.rs#308)/// // It can be read multiple times
[309](https://docs.rs#309)/// assert_eq!(42, **arc_swap.load());
[310](https://docs.rs#310)///
[311](https://docs.rs#311)/// // Put a new one in there
[312](https://docs.rs#312)/// let new_arc = Arc::new(0);
[313](https://docs.rs#313)/// assert_eq!(42, *arc_swap.swap(new_arc));
[314](https://docs.rs#314)/// assert_eq!(0, **arc_swap.load());
[315](https://docs.rs#315)/// ```
[316](https://docs.rs#316)///
[317](https://docs.rs#317)/// # Known bugs
[318](https://docs.rs#318)///
[319](https://docs.rs#319)/// Currently, things like `ArcSwapAny<Option<Option<Arc<_>>>>` (notice the double Option) don't
[320](https://docs.rs#320)/// work properly. A proper solution is being looked into
[321](https://docs.rs#321)/// ([#81](https://github.com/vorner/arc-swap/issues)).
[322](https://docs.rs#322)///
[323](https://docs.rs#323)/// [`Arc`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html
[324](https://docs.rs#324)/// [`from`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/convert/trait.From.html#tymethod.from
[325](https://docs.rs#325)/// [`RefCnt`]: trait.RefCnt.html
[326](https://docs.rs#326)pub struct ArcSwapAny<T: RefCnt, S: Strategy<T> = DefaultStrategy> {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    // Notes: AtomicPtr needs Sized
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    /// The actual pointer, extracted from the Arc.
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    ptr: AtomicPtr<T::Base>,
[330](https://docs.rs#330)
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    /// We are basically an Arc in disguise. Inherit parameters from Arc by pretending to contain
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    /// it.
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    _phantom_arc: PhantomData<T>,
[334](https://docs.rs#334)
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    /// Strategy to protect the data.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    strategy: S,
[337](https://docs.rs#337)}
[338](https://docs.rs#338)
[339](https://docs.rs#339)impl<T: RefCnt, S: Default + Strategy<T>> From<T> for ArcSwapAny<T, S> {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    fn from(val: T) -> Self {
[341](https://docs.rs#341)        Self::with_strategy(val, S::default())
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    }
[343](https://docs.rs#343)}
[344](https://docs.rs#344)
[345](https://docs.rs#345)impl<T: RefCnt, S: Strategy<T>> Drop for ArcSwapAny<T, S> {
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    fn drop(&mut self) {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        let ptr = *self.ptr.get_mut();
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        unsafe {
[349](https://docs.rs#349)            // To pay any possible debts
[350](https://docs.rs#350)            self.strategy.wait_for_readers(ptr, &self.ptr);
[351](https://docs.rs#351)            // We are getting rid of the one stored ref count
[352](https://docs.rs#352)            T::dec(ptr);
[353](https://docs.rs#353)        }
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    }
[355](https://docs.rs#355)}

[357](https://docs.rs#357)impl<T, S: Strategy<T>> Debug for ArcSwapAny<T, S>

[360](https://docs.rs#360){

[378](https://docs.rs#378)impl<T: RefCnt + Default, S: Default + Strategy<T>> Default for ArcSwapAny<T, S> {
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    fn default() -> Self {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        Self::new(T::default())
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)}
[383](https://docs.rs#383)
[384](https://docs.rs#384)impl<T: RefCnt, S: Strategy<T>> ArcSwapAny<T, S> {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    /// Constructs a new storage.
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    pub fn new(val: T) -> Self
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    where
[388](https://docs.rs#388)        S: Default,
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    {
[390](https://docs.rs#390)        Self::from(val)
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    }
[392](https://docs.rs#392)
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// Constructs a new storage while customizing the protection strategy.
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    pub fn with_strategy(val: T, strategy: S) -> Self {
[395](https://docs.rs#395)        // The AtomicPtr requires *mut in its interface. We are more like *const, so we cast it.
[396](https://docs.rs#396)        // However, we always go back to *const right away when we get the pointer on the other
[397](https://docs.rs#397)        // side, so it should be fine.
[398](https://docs.rs#398)        let ptr = T::into_ptr(val);
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        Self {
[400](https://docs.rs#400)            ptr: AtomicPtr::new(ptr),
[401](https://docs.rs#401)            _phantom_arc: PhantomData,
[402](https://docs.rs#402)            strategy,
[403](https://docs.rs#403)        }
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    }
[405](https://docs.rs#405)
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// Extracts the value inside.
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    pub fn into_inner(mut self) -> T {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)        let ptr = *self.ptr.get_mut();
[409](https://docs.rs#409)        // To pay all the debts
[410](https://docs.rs#410)        unsafe { self.strategy.wait_for_readers(ptr, &self.ptr) };
[411](https://docs.rs#411)        mem::forget(self);
[412](https://docs.rs#412)        unsafe { T::from_ptr(ptr) }
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    }
[414](https://docs.rs#414)
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// Loads the value.
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    ///
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// This makes another copy of the held pointer and returns it, atomically (it is
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    /// safe even when other thread stores into the same instance at the same time).
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    ///
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// The method is lock-free and wait-free, but usually more expensive than
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// [`load`](#method.load).
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    pub fn load_full(&self) -> T {
[423](https://docs.rs#423)        Guard::into_inner(self.load())
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    }
[425](https://docs.rs#425)
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// Provides a temporary borrow of the object inside.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// This returns a proxy object allowing access to the thing held inside. However, there's
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// only limited amount of possible cheap proxies in existence for each thread ‒ if more are
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// created, it falls back to equivalent of [`load_full`](#method.load_full) internally.
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    ///
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// This is therefore a good choice to use for eg. searching a data structure or juggling the
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// pointers around a bit, but not as something to store in larger amounts. The rule of thumb
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// is this is suited for local variables on stack, but not in long-living data structures.
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    ///
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// # Consistency
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    ///
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// In case multiple related operations are to be done on the loaded value, it is generally
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// recommended to call `load` just once and keep the result over calling it multiple times.
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// First, keeping it is usually faster. But more importantly, the value can change between the
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// calls to load, returning different objects, which could lead to logical inconsistency.
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    /// Keeping the result makes sure the same object is used.
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    ///
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    /// ```rust
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    /// # use arc_swap::ArcSwap;
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// struct Point {
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    ///     x: usize,
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    ///     y: usize,
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    /// }
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    ///
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// fn print_broken(p: &ArcSwap<Point>) {
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    ///     // This is broken, because the x and y may come from different points,
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    ///     // combining into an invalid point that never existed.
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    ///     println!("X: {}", p.load().x);
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    ///     // If someone changes the content now, between these two loads, we
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    ///     // have a problem
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    ///     println!("Y: {}", p.load().y);
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    /// }
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    ///
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// fn print_correct(p: &ArcSwap<Point>) {
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    ///     // Here we take a snapshot of one specific point so both x and y come
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    ///     // from the same one.
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    ///     let point = p.load();
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    ///     println!("X: {}", point.x);
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    ///     println!("Y: {}", point.y);
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    /// }
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// # let p = ArcSwap::from_pointee(Point { x: 10, y: 20 });
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    /// # print_correct(&p);
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    /// # print_broken(&p);
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    /// ```
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    #[inline]
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    pub fn load(&self) -> Guard<T, S> {
[473](https://docs.rs#473)        let protected = unsafe { self.strategy.load(&self.ptr) };
[474](https://docs.rs#474)        Guard { inner: protected }
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    }
[476](https://docs.rs#476)
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    /// Replaces the value inside this instance.
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    ///
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    /// Further loads will yield the new value. Uses [`swap`](#method.swap) internally.
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    pub fn store(&self, val: T) {
[481](https://docs.rs#481)        drop(self.swap(val));
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    }
[483](https://docs.rs#483)
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    /// Exchanges the value inside this instance.
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    pub fn swap(&self, new: T) -> T {
[486](https://docs.rs#486)        let new = T::into_ptr(new);
[487](https://docs.rs#487)        // AcqRel needed to publish the target of the new pointer and get the target of the old
[488](https://docs.rs#488)        // one.
[489](https://docs.rs#489)        //
[490](https://docs.rs#490)        // SeqCst to synchronize the time lines with the group counters.
[491](https://docs.rs#491)        let old = self.ptr.swap(new, Ordering::SeqCst);
[492](https://docs.rs#492)        unsafe {
[493](https://docs.rs#493)            self.strategy.wait_for_readers(old, &self.ptr);
[494](https://docs.rs#494)            T::from_ptr(old)
[495](https://docs.rs#495)        }
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    }
[497](https://docs.rs#497)
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    /// Swaps the stored Arc if it equals to `current`.
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    ///
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    /// If the current value of the `ArcSwapAny` equals to `current`, the `new` is stored inside.
[501](https://docs.rs#501)    /// If not, nothing happens.
[502](https://docs.rs#502)    ///
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    /// The previous value (no matter if the swap happened or not) is returned. Therefore, if the
[504](https://docs.rs#504)    /// returned value is equal to `current`, the swap happened. You want to do a pointer-based
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    /// comparison to determine it.
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    ///
[507](https://docs.rs#507)    /// In other words, if the caller „guesses“ the value of current correctly, it acts like
[508](https://docs.rs#508)    /// [`swap`](#method.swap), otherwise it acts like [`load_full`](#method.load_full) (including
[509](https://docs.rs#509)    /// the limitations).
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    ///
[511](https://docs.rs#511)    /// The `current` can be specified as `&Arc`, [`Guard`](struct.Guard.html),
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    /// [`&Guards`](struct.Guards.html) or as a raw pointer (but _not_ owned `Arc`). See the
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    /// [`AsRaw`] trait.
[514](https://docs.rs#514)    pub fn compare_and_swap<C>(&self, current: C, new: T) -> Guard<T, S>
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    where
[516](https://docs.rs#516)        C: AsRaw<T::Base>,
[517](https://docs.rs#517)        S: CaS<T>,
[518](https://docs.rs#518)    {
[519](https://docs.rs#519)        let protected = unsafe { self.strategy.compare_and_swap(&self.ptr, current, new) };
[520](https://docs.rs#520)        Guard { inner: protected }
[521](https://docs.rs#521)    }
[522](https://docs.rs#522)
[523](https://docs.rs#523)    /// Read-Copy-Update of the pointer inside.
[524](https://docs.rs#524)    ///
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    /// This is useful in read-heavy situations with several threads that sometimes update the data
[526](https://docs.rs#526)    /// pointed to. The readers can just repeatedly use [`load`](#method.load) without any locking.
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    /// The writer uses this method to perform the update.
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    ///
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    /// In case there's only one thread that does updates or in case the next version is
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    /// independent of the previous one, simple [`swap`](#method.swap) or [`store`](#method.store)
[531](https://docs.rs#531)    /// is enough. Otherwise, it may be needed to retry the update operation if some other thread
[532](https://docs.rs#532)    /// made an update in between. This is what this method does.
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    ///
[534](https://docs.rs#534)    /// # Examples
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    ///
[536](https://docs.rs#536)    /// This will *not* work as expected, because between loading and storing, some other thread
[537](https://docs.rs#537)    /// might have updated the value.
[538](https://docs.rs#538)    ///
[539](https://docs.rs#539)    /// ```rust
[540](https://docs.rs#540)    /// # use std::sync::Arc;
[541](https://docs.rs#541)    /// #
[542](https://docs.rs#542)    /// # use arc_swap::ArcSwap;
[543](https://docs.rs#543)    /// # use crossbeam_utils::thread;
[544](https://docs.rs#544)    /// #
[545](https://docs.rs#545)    /// let cnt = ArcSwap::from_pointee(0);
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    /// thread::scope(|scope| {
[547](https://docs.rs#547)    ///     for _ in 0..10 {
[548](https://docs.rs#548)    ///         scope.spawn(|_| {
[549](https://docs.rs#549)    ///            let inner = cnt.load_full();
[550](https://docs.rs#550)    ///             // Another thread might have stored some other number than what we have
[551](https://docs.rs#551)    ///             // between the load and store.
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    ///             cnt.store(Arc::new(*inner + 1));
[553](https://docs.rs#553)    ///         });
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    ///     }
[555](https://docs.rs#555)    /// }).unwrap();
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    /// // This will likely fail:
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    /// // assert_eq!(10, *cnt.load_full());
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    /// ```
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    ///
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    /// This will, but it can call the closure multiple times to retry:
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    ///
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    /// ```rust
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    /// # use arc_swap::ArcSwap;
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    /// # use crossbeam_utils::thread;
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    /// #
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    /// let cnt = ArcSwap::from_pointee(0);
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    /// thread::scope(|scope| {
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    ///     for _ in 0..10 {
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    ///         scope.spawn(|_| cnt.rcu(|inner| **inner + 1));
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    ///     }
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    /// }).unwrap();
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    /// assert_eq!(10, *cnt.load_full());
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    /// ```
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    ///
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    /// Due to the retries, you might want to perform all the expensive operations *before* the
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    /// rcu. As an example, if there's a cache of some computations as a map, and the map is cheap
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    /// to clone but the computations are not, you could do something like this:
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    ///
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    /// ```rust
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// # use std::collections::HashMap;
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    /// #
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    /// # use arc_swap::ArcSwap;
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    /// # use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    /// #
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    /// fn expensive_computation(x: usize) -> usize {
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    ///     x * 2 // Let's pretend multiplication is *really expensive expensive*
[587](https://docs.rs#587)    /// }
[588](https://docs.rs#588)    ///
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    /// type Cache = HashMap<usize, usize>;
[590](https://docs.rs#590)    ///
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    /// static CACHE: Lazy<ArcSwap<Cache>> = Lazy::new(|| ArcSwap::default());
[592](https://docs.rs#592)    ///
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    /// fn cached_computation(x: usize) -> usize {
[594](https://docs.rs#594)    ///     let cache = CACHE.load();
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    ///     if let Some(result) = cache.get(&x) {
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    ///         return *result;
[597](https://docs.rs#597)    ///     }
[598](https://docs.rs#598)    ///     // Not in cache. Compute and store.
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    ///     // The expensive computation goes outside, so it is not retried.
[600](https://docs.rs#600)    ///     let result = expensive_computation(x);
[601](https://docs.rs#601)    ///     CACHE.rcu(|cache| {
[602](https://docs.rs#602)    ///         // The cheaper clone of the cache can be retried if need be.
[603](https://docs.rs#603)    ///         let mut cache = HashMap::clone(&cache);
[604](https://docs.rs#604)    ///         cache.insert(x, result);
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    ///         cache
[606](https://docs.rs#606)    ///     });
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    ///     result
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    /// }
[609](https://docs.rs#609)    ///
[610](https://docs.rs#610)    /// assert_eq!(42, cached_computation(21));
[611](https://docs.rs#611)    /// assert_eq!(42, cached_computation(21));
[612](https://docs.rs#612)    /// ```
[613](https://docs.rs#613)    ///
[614](https://docs.rs#614)    /// # The cost of cloning
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    ///
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    /// Depending on the size of cache above, the cloning might not be as cheap. You can however
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    /// use persistent data structures ‒ each modification creates a new data structure, but it
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    /// shares most of the data with the old one (which is usually accomplished by using `Arc`s
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    /// inside to share the unchanged values). Something like
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    /// [`rpds`](https://crates.io/crates/rpds) or [`im`](https://crates.io/crates/im) might do
[621](https://docs.rs#621)    /// what you need.
[622](https://docs.rs#622)    pub fn rcu<R, F>(&self, mut f: F) -> T
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    where
[624](https://docs.rs#624)        F: FnMut(&T) -> R,
[625](https://docs.rs#625)        R: Into<T>,
[626](https://docs.rs#626)        S: CaS<T>,
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    {
[628](https://docs.rs#628)        let mut cur = self.load();
[629](https://docs.rs#629)        loop {
[630](https://docs.rs#630)            let new = f(&cur).into();
[631](https://docs.rs#631)            let prev = self.compare_and_swap(&*cur, new);
[632](https://docs.rs#632)            let swapped = ptr_eq(&*cur, &*prev);
[633](https://docs.rs#633)            if swapped {
[634](https://docs.rs#634)                return Guard::into_inner(prev);
[635](https://docs.rs#635)            } else {
[636](https://docs.rs#636)                cur = prev;
[637](https://docs.rs#637)            }
[638](https://docs.rs#638)        }
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    }
[640](https://docs.rs#640)
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// Provides an access to an up to date projection of the carried data.
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    ///
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    /// # Motivation
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    ///
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// Sometimes, an application consists of components. Each component has its own configuration
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    /// structure. The whole configuration contains all the smaller config parts.
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    ///
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    /// For the sake of separation and abstraction, it is not desirable to pass the whole
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    /// configuration to each of the components. This allows the component to take only access to
[650](https://docs.rs#650)    /// its own part.
[651](https://docs.rs#651)    ///
[652](https://docs.rs#652)    /// # Lifetimes & flexibility
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    ///
[654](https://docs.rs#654)    /// This method is not the most flexible way, as the returned type borrows into the `ArcSwap`.
[655](https://docs.rs#655)    /// To provide access into eg. `Arc<ArcSwap<T>>`, you can create the [`Map`] type directly. See
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    /// the [`access`] module.
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    ///
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    /// # Performance
[659](https://docs.rs#659)    ///
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    /// As the provided function is called on each load from the shared storage, it should
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    /// generally be cheap. It is expected this will usually be just referencing of a field inside
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    /// the structure.
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    ///
[664](https://docs.rs#664)    /// # Examples
[665](https://docs.rs#665)    ///
[666](https://docs.rs#666)    /// ```rust
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    /// use std::sync::Arc;
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    ///
[669](https://docs.rs#669)    /// use arc_swap::ArcSwap;
[670](https://docs.rs#670)    /// use arc_swap::access::Access;
[671](https://docs.rs#671)    ///
[672](https://docs.rs#672)    /// struct Cfg {
[673](https://docs.rs#673)    ///     value: usize,
[674](https://docs.rs#674)    /// }
[675](https://docs.rs#675)    ///
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    /// fn print_many_times<V: Access<usize>>(value: V) {
[677](https://docs.rs#677)    ///     for _ in 0..25 {
[678](https://docs.rs#678)    ///         let value = value.load();
[679](https://docs.rs#679)    ///         println!("{}", *value);
[680](https://docs.rs#680)    ///     }
[681](https://docs.rs#681)    /// }
[682](https://docs.rs#682)    ///
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    /// let shared = ArcSwap::from_pointee(Cfg { value: 0 });
[684](https://docs.rs#684)    /// let mapped = shared.map(|c: &Cfg| &c.value);
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    /// crossbeam_utils::thread::scope(|s| {
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    ///     // Will print some zeroes and some twos
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    ///     s.spawn(|_| print_many_times(mapped));
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    ///     s.spawn(|_| shared.store(Arc::new(Cfg { value: 2 })));
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    /// }).expect("Something panicked in a thread");
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    /// ```
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    pub fn map<I, R, F>(&self, f: F) -> Map<&Self, I, F>
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    where
[693](https://docs.rs#693)        F: Fn(&I) -> &R + Clone,
[694](https://docs.rs#694)        Self: Access<I>,
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    {
[696](https://docs.rs#696)        Map::new(self, f)
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    }
[698](https://docs.rs#698)}
[699](https://docs.rs#699)

[855](https://docs.rs#855)                for _ in 0..ITERATIONS {

[857](https://docs.rs#857)                    let ended = AtomicUsize::new(0);
[858](https://docs.rs#858)                    thread::scope(|scope| {

[864](https://docs.rs#864)                                    ended.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
[865](https://docs.rs#865)                                    return;

[868](https://docs.rs#868)                            });
[869](https://docs.rs#869)                        }

[906](https://docs.rs#906)
[907](https://docs.rs#907)            /// Two different writers publish two series of values. The readers check that it is
[908](https://docs.rs#908)            /// always increasing in each series.
[909](https://docs.rs#909)            ///
[910](https://docs.rs#910)            /// For performance, we try to reuse the threads here.
[911](https://docs.rs#911)            #[test]
[912](https://docs.rs#912)            fn multi_writers() {
[913](https://docs.rs#913)                let first_value = Arc::new((0, 0));
[914](https://docs.rs#914)                let shared = As::from(Arc::clone(&first_value));
[915](https://docs.rs#915)                const WRITER_CNT: usize = 2;
[916](https://docs.rs#916)                const READER_CNT: usize = 3;
[917](https://docs.rs#917)                #[cfg(miri)]
[918](https://docs.rs#918)                const ITERATIONS: usize = 5;
[919](https://docs.rs#919)                #[cfg(not(miri))]
[920](https://docs.rs#920)                const ITERATIONS: usize = 100;
[921](https://docs.rs#921)                const SEQ: usize = 50;
[922](https://docs.rs#922)                let barrier = Barrier::new(PanicMode::Poison);
[923](https://docs.rs#923)                thread::scope(|scope| {
[924](https://docs.rs#924)                    for w in 0..WRITER_CNT {
[925](https://docs.rs#925)                        // We need to move w into the closure. But we want to just reference the
[926](https://docs.rs#926)                        // other things.
[927](https://docs.rs#927)                        let mut barrier = barrier.clone();
[928](https://docs.rs#928)                        let shared = &shared;
[929](https://docs.rs#929)                        let first_value = &first_value;
[930](https://docs.rs#930)                        scope.spawn(move |_| {
[931](https://docs.rs#931)                            for _ in 0..ITERATIONS {
[932](https://docs.rs#932)                                barrier.wait();
[933](https://docs.rs#933)                                shared.store(Arc::clone(&first_value));
[934](https://docs.rs#934)                                barrier.wait();
[935](https://docs.rs#935)                                for i in 0..SEQ {
[936](https://docs.rs#936)                                    shared.store(Arc::new((w, i + 1)));
[937](https://docs.rs#937)                                }
[938](https://docs.rs#938)                            }
[939](https://docs.rs#939)                        });
[940](https://docs.rs#940)                    }
[941](https://docs.rs#941)                    for _ in 0..READER_CNT {
[942](https://docs.rs#942)                        let mut barrier = barrier.clone();
[943](https://docs.rs#943)                        let shared = &shared;
[944](https://docs.rs#944)                        let first_value = &first_value;
[945](https://docs.rs#945)                        scope.spawn(move |_| {
[946](https://docs.rs#946)                            for _ in 0..ITERATIONS {
[947](https://docs.rs#947)                                barrier.wait();
[948](https://docs.rs#948)                                barrier.wait();
[949](https://docs.rs#949)                                let mut previous = [0; WRITER_CNT];
[950](https://docs.rs#950)                                let mut last = Arc::clone(&first_value);
[951](https://docs.rs#951)                                loop {
[952](https://docs.rs#952)                                    let cur = shared.load();
[953](https://docs.rs#953)                                    if Arc::ptr_eq(&last, &cur) {
[954](https://docs.rs#954)                                        atomic::spin_loop_hint();
[955](https://docs.rs#955)                                        continue;
[956](https://docs.rs#956)                                    }
[957](https://docs.rs#957)                                    let (w, s) = **cur;
[958](https://docs.rs#958)                                    assert!(previous[w] < s, "{:?} vs {:?}", previous, cur);
[959](https://docs.rs#959)                                    previous[w] = s;
[960](https://docs.rs#960)                                    last = Guard::into_inner(cur);
[961](https://docs.rs#961)                                    if s == SEQ {
[962](https://docs.rs#962)                                        break;
[963](https://docs.rs#963)                                    }
[964](https://docs.rs#964)                                }
[965](https://docs.rs#965)                            }
[966](https://docs.rs#966)                        });
[967](https://docs.rs#967)                    }

[995](https://docs.rs#995)            // Note on the Relaxed order here. This should be enough, because there's that
[996](https://docs.rs#996)            // barrier.wait in between that should do the synchronization of happens-before for us.
[997](https://docs.rs#997)            // And using SeqCst would probably not help either, as there's nothing else with SeqCst
[998](https://docs.rs#998)            // here in this test to relate it to.
[999](https://docs.rs#999)            #[derive(Default)]
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)            struct ReportDrop(Arc<AtomicUsize>);
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)            impl Drop for ReportDrop {
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)                fn drop(&mut self) {
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)                    self.0.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)                }
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)            }
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)            /// Interaction of two threads about a guard and dropping it.
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)            ///
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)            /// We make sure everything works in timely manner (eg. dropping of stuff) even if multiple
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)            /// threads interact.
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)            ///
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)            /// The idea is:
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)            /// * Thread 1 loads a value.
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)            /// * Thread 2 replaces the shared value. The original value is not destroyed.
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)            /// * Thread 1 drops the guard. The value is destroyed and this is observable in both threads.
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)            #[test]
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)            fn guard_drop_in_thread() {
[1018](https://docs.rs#1018)                for _ in 0..ITERATIONS {
[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)                    let cnt = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)                    let shared = As::from_pointee(ReportDrop(cnt.clone()));
[1022](https://docs.rs#1022)                    assert_eq!(cnt.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 0, "Dropped prematurely");
[1023](https://docs.rs#1023)                    // We need the threads to wait for each other at places.
[1024](https://docs.rs#1024)                    let sync = Barrier::new(PanicMode::Poison);
[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)                    thread::scope(|scope| {
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)                        scope.spawn({
[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)                            let sync = sync.clone();
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)                            |_| {
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)                                let mut sync = sync; // Move into the closure
[1031](https://docs.rs#1031)                                let guard = shared.load();
[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)                                sync.wait();
[1033](https://docs.rs#1033)                                // Thread 2 replaces the shared value. We wait for it to confirm.
[1034](https://docs.rs#1034)                                sync.wait();
[1035](https://docs.rs#1035)                                drop(guard);
[1036](https://docs.rs#1036)                                assert_eq!(cnt.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 1, "Value not dropped");
[1037](https://docs.rs#1037)                                // Let thread 2 know we already dropped it.
[1038](https://docs.rs#1038)                                sync.wait();
[1039](https://docs.rs#1039)                            }
[1040](https://docs.rs#1040)                        });
[1041](https://docs.rs#1041)
[1042](https://docs.rs#1042)                        scope.spawn(|_| {
[1043](https://docs.rs#1043)                            let mut sync = sync;
[1044](https://docs.rs#1044)                            // Thread 1 loads, we wait for that
[1045](https://docs.rs#1045)                            sync.wait();
[1046](https://docs.rs#1046)                            shared.store(Default::default());
[1047](https://docs.rs#1047)                            assert_eq!(
[1048](https://docs.rs#1048)                                cnt.load(Ordering::Relaxed),
[1049](https://docs.rs#1049)                                0,
[1050](https://docs.rs#1050)                                "Dropped while still in use"
[1051](https://docs.rs#1051)                            );
[1052](https://docs.rs#1052)                            // Let thread 2 know we replaced it
[1053](https://docs.rs#1053)                            sync.wait();
[1054](https://docs.rs#1054)                            // Thread 1 drops its guard. We wait for it to confirm.
[1055](https://docs.rs#1055)                            sync.wait();
[1056](https://docs.rs#1056)                            assert_eq!(cnt.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 1, "Value not dropped");
[1057](https://docs.rs#1057)                        });
[1058](https://docs.rs#1058)                    })
[1059](https://docs.rs#1059)                    .unwrap();
[1060](https://docs.rs#1060)                }
[1061](https://docs.rs#1061)            }
[1062](https://docs.rs#1062)
[1063](https://docs.rs#1063)            /// Check dropping a lease in a different thread than it was created doesn't cause any
[1064](https://docs.rs#1064)            /// problems.
[1065](https://docs.rs#1065)            #[test]
[1066](https://docs.rs#1066)            fn guard_drop_in_another_thread() {
[1067](https://docs.rs#1067)                for _ in 0..ITERATIONS {
[1068](https://docs.rs#1068)                    let cnt = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
[1069](https://docs.rs#1069)                    let shared = As::from_pointee(ReportDrop(cnt.clone()));
[1070](https://docs.rs#1070)                    assert_eq!(cnt.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 0, "Dropped prematurely");
[1071](https://docs.rs#1071)                    let guard = shared.load();
[1072](https://docs.rs#1072)
[1073](https://docs.rs#1073)                    drop(shared);
[1074](https://docs.rs#1074)                    assert_eq!(cnt.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 0, "Dropped prematurely");
[1075](https://docs.rs#1075)
[1076](https://docs.rs#1076)                    thread::scope(|scope| {
[1077](https://docs.rs#1077)                        scope.spawn(|_| {
[1078](https://docs.rs#1078)                            drop(guard);
[1079](https://docs.rs#1079)                        });
[1080](https://docs.rs#1080)                    })
[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)                    .unwrap();
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)                    assert_eq!(cnt.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 1, "Not dropped");
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)                }
[1085](https://docs.rs#1085)            }

[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)            #[test]
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)            /// Make sure the reference count and compare_and_swap works as expected.
[1196](https://docs.rs#1196)            fn cas_ref_cnt() {
[1197](https://docs.rs#1197)                #[cfg(miri)]
[1198](https://docs.rs#1198)                const ITERATIONS: usize = 10;
[1199](https://docs.rs#1199)                #[cfg(not(miri))]
[1200](https://docs.rs#1200)                const ITERATIONS: usize = 50;
[1201](https://docs.rs#1201)                let shared = ArcSwap::from(Arc::new(0));
[1202](https://docs.rs#1202)                for i in 0..ITERATIONS {
[1203](https://docs.rs#1203)                    let orig = shared.load_full();
[1204](https://docs.rs#1204)                    assert_eq!(i, *orig);
[1205](https://docs.rs#1205)                    if i % 2 == 1 {
[1206](https://docs.rs#1206)                        // One for orig, one for shared
[1207](https://docs.rs#1207)                        assert_eq!(2, Arc::strong_count(&orig));
[1208](https://docs.rs#1208)                    }
[1209](https://docs.rs#1209)                    let n1 = Arc::new(i + 1);
[1210](https://docs.rs#1210)                    // Fill up the slots sometimes
[1211](https://docs.rs#1211)                    let fillup = || {
[1212](https://docs.rs#1212)                        if i % 2 == 0 {
[1213](https://docs.rs#1213)                            Some((0..ITERATIONS).map(|_| shared.load()).collect::<Vec<_>>())
[1214](https://docs.rs#1214)                        } else {
[1215](https://docs.rs#1215)                            None
[1216](https://docs.rs#1216)                        }
[1217](https://docs.rs#1217)                    };
[1218](https://docs.rs#1218)                    let guards = fillup();
[1219](https://docs.rs#1219)                    // Success
[1220](https://docs.rs#1220)                    let prev = shared.compare_and_swap(&orig, Arc::clone(&n1));
[1221](https://docs.rs#1221)                    assert!(ptr_eq(&orig, &prev));
[1222](https://docs.rs#1222)                    drop(guards);
[1223](https://docs.rs#1223)                    // One for orig, one for prev
[1224](https://docs.rs#1224)                    assert_eq!(2, Arc::strong_count(&orig));
[1225](https://docs.rs#1225)                    // One for n1, one for shared
[1226](https://docs.rs#1226)                    assert_eq!(2, Arc::strong_count(&n1));
[1227](https://docs.rs#1227)                    assert_eq!(i + 1, **shared.load());
[1228](https://docs.rs#1228)                    let n2 = Arc::new(i);
[1229](https://docs.rs#1229)                    drop(prev);
[1230](https://docs.rs#1230)                    let guards = fillup();
[1231](https://docs.rs#1231)                    // Failure
[1232](https://docs.rs#1232)                    let prev = Guard::into_inner(shared.compare_and_swap(&orig, Arc::clone(&n2)));
[1233](https://docs.rs#1233)                    drop(guards);
[1234](https://docs.rs#1234)                    assert!(ptr_eq(&n1, &prev));
[1235](https://docs.rs#1235)                    // One for orig
[1236](https://docs.rs#1236)                    assert_eq!(1, Arc::strong_count(&orig));
[1237](https://docs.rs#1237)                    // One for n1, one for shared, one for prev
[1238](https://docs.rs#1238)                    assert_eq!(3, Arc::strong_count(&n1));
[1239](https://docs.rs#1239)                    // n2 didn't get increased
[1240](https://docs.rs#1240)                    assert_eq!(1, Arc::strong_count(&n2));
[1241](https://docs.rs#1241)                    assert_eq!(i + 1, **shared.load());
[1242](https://docs.rs#1242)                }
[1243](https://docs.rs#1243)
[1244](https://docs.rs#1244)                let a = shared.load_full();
[1245](https://docs.rs#1245)                // One inside shared, one for a
[1246](https://docs.rs#1246)                assert_eq!(2, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1247](https://docs.rs#1247)                drop(shared);
[1248](https://docs.rs#1248)                // Only a now
[1249](https://docs.rs#1249)                assert_eq!(1, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1250](https://docs.rs#1250)            }
[1251](https://docs.rs#1251)        }

[1273](https://docs.rs#1273)    /// Accessing the value inside ArcSwap with Guards (and checks for the reference
[1274](https://docs.rs#1274)    /// counts).
[1275](https://docs.rs#1275)    #[test]
[1276](https://docs.rs#1276)    fn load_cnt() {
[1277](https://docs.rs#1277)        let a = Arc::new(0);
[1278](https://docs.rs#1278)        let shared = ArcSwap::from(Arc::clone(&a));
[1279](https://docs.rs#1279)        // One in shared, one in a
[1280](https://docs.rs#1280)        assert_eq!(2, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1281](https://docs.rs#1281)        let guard = shared.load();
[1282](https://docs.rs#1282)        assert_eq!(0, **guard);
[1283](https://docs.rs#1283)        // The guard doesn't have its own ref count now
[1284](https://docs.rs#1284)        assert_eq!(2, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1285](https://docs.rs#1285)        let guard_2 = shared.load();
[1286](https://docs.rs#1286)        // Unlike with guard, this does not deadlock
[1287](https://docs.rs#1287)        shared.store(Arc::new(1));
[1288](https://docs.rs#1288)        // But now, each guard got a full Arc inside it
[1289](https://docs.rs#1289)        assert_eq!(3, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1290](https://docs.rs#1290)        // And when we get rid of them, they disappear
[1291](https://docs.rs#1291)        drop(guard_2);
[1292](https://docs.rs#1292)        assert_eq!(2, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1293](https://docs.rs#1293)        let _b = Arc::clone(&guard);
[1294](https://docs.rs#1294)        assert_eq!(3, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1295](https://docs.rs#1295)        // We can drop the guard it came from
[1296](https://docs.rs#1296)        drop(guard);
[1297](https://docs.rs#1297)        assert_eq!(2, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1298](https://docs.rs#1298)        let guard = shared.load();
[1299](https://docs.rs#1299)        assert_eq!(1, **guard);
[1300](https://docs.rs#1300)        drop(shared);
[1301](https://docs.rs#1301)        // We can still use the guard after the shared disappears
[1302](https://docs.rs#1302)        assert_eq!(1, **guard);
[1303](https://docs.rs#1303)        let ptr = Arc::clone(&guard);
[1304](https://docs.rs#1304)        // One in shared, one in guard
[1305](https://docs.rs#1305)        assert_eq!(2, Arc::strong_count(&ptr));
[1306](https://docs.rs#1306)        drop(guard);
[1307](https://docs.rs#1307)        assert_eq!(1, Arc::strong_count(&ptr));
[1308](https://docs.rs#1308)    }

[1310](https://docs.rs#1310)    /// There can be only limited amount of leases on one thread. Following ones are
[1311](https://docs.rs#1311)    /// created, but contain full Arcs.
[1312](https://docs.rs#1312)    #[test]
[1313](https://docs.rs#1313)    fn lease_overflow() {
[1314](https://docs.rs#1314)        #[cfg(miri)]
[1315](https://docs.rs#1315)        const GUARD_COUNT: usize = 100;
[1316](https://docs.rs#1316)        #[cfg(not(miri))]
[1317](https://docs.rs#1317)        const GUARD_COUNT: usize = 1000;
[1318](https://docs.rs#1318)        let a = Arc::new(0);
[1319](https://docs.rs#1319)        let shared = ArcSwap::from(Arc::clone(&a));
[1320](https://docs.rs#1320)        assert_eq!(2, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1321](https://docs.rs#1321)        let mut guards = (0..GUARD_COUNT).map(|_| shared.load()).collect::<Vec<_>>();
[1322](https://docs.rs#1322)        let count = Arc::strong_count(&a);
[1323](https://docs.rs#1323)        assert!(count > 2);
[1324](https://docs.rs#1324)        let guard = shared.load();
[1325](https://docs.rs#1325)        assert_eq!(count + 1, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1326](https://docs.rs#1326)        drop(guard);
[1327](https://docs.rs#1327)        assert_eq!(count, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1328](https://docs.rs#1328)        // When we delete the first one, it didn't have an Arc in it, so the ref count
[1329](https://docs.rs#1329)        // doesn't drop
[1330](https://docs.rs#1330)        guards.swap_remove(0);
[1331](https://docs.rs#1331)        assert_eq!(count, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1332](https://docs.rs#1332)        // But new one reuses now vacant the slot and doesn't create a new Arc
[1333](https://docs.rs#1333)        let _guard = shared.load();
[1334](https://docs.rs#1334)        assert_eq!(count, Arc::strong_count(&a));
[1335](https://docs.rs#1335)    }

# ArcSwapAny in arc_swap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arc-swap/1.9.2/arc_swap/struct.ArcSwapAny.html

`pub struct ArcSwapAny<T: `[RefCnt](https://docs.rs/trait.RefCnt.html), S: [Strategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/trait.Strategy.html)<T> = [DefaultStrategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/type.DefaultStrategy.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

An atomic storage for a reference counted smart pointer like [ Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html) or

`Option<Arc>`.This is a storage where a smart pointer may live. It can be read and written atomically from several threads, but doesn’t act like a pointer itself.

One can be created [ from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/convert/trait.From.html#tymethod.from) an

[. To get the pointer back, use the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html)

`Arc`[.](https://docs.rs#method.load)

`load`[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

This is the common generic implementation. This allows sharing the same code for storing
both `Arc` and `Option<Arc>` (and possibly other similar types).

In your code, you most probably want to interact with it through the
[ ArcSwap](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwap.html) and

[aliases. However, the methods they share are described here and are applicable to both of them. That’s why the examples here use](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwapOption.html)

`ArcSwapOption``ArcSwap` ‒ but they could as well be written with `ArcSwapOption` or
`ArcSwapAny`.[§](https://docs.rs#type-parameters)Type parameters

- `T`: The smart pointer to be kept inside. This crate provides implementation for- `Arc<_>`and- `Option<Arc<_>>`(- `Rc`too, but that one is not practically useful). But third party could provide implementations of the- `RefCnt`
- `S`: Chooses the- [strategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/index.html)used to protect the data inside. They come with various performance trade offs, the default- `DefaultStrategy`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let arc = Arc::new(42);
let arc_swap = ArcSwap::from(arc);
assert_eq!(42, **arc_swap.load());
// It can be read multiple times
assert_eq!(42, **arc_swap.load());
// Put a new one in there
let new_arc = Arc::new(0);
assert_eq!(42, *arc_swap.swap(new_arc));
assert_eq!(0, **arc_swap.load());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#known-bugs)Known bugs

Currently, things like `ArcSwapAny<Option<Option<Arc<_>>>>` (notice the double Option) don’t
work properly. A proper solution is being looked into
([#81](https://github.com/vorner/arc-swap/issues)).

### impl<T: [RefCnt](https://docs.rs/trait.RefCnt.html), S: [Strategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/trait.Strategy.html)<T>> [ArcSwapAny](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html)<T, S>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arc_swap/lib.rs.html#394-404)#### pub fn [with_strategy](https://docs.rs#method.with_strategy)(val: T, strategy: S) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arc_swap/lib.rs.html#394-404)

#### pub fn [with_strategy](https://docs.rs#method.with_strategy)(val: T, strategy: S) -> Self

Constructs a new storage while customizing the protection strategy.

Loads the value.

This makes another copy of the held pointer and returns it, atomically (it is safe even when other thread stores into the same instance at the same time).

The method is lock-free and wait-free, but usually more expensive than
[ load](https://docs.rs#method.load).

Provides a temporary borrow of the object inside.

This returns a proxy object allowing access to the thing held inside. However, there’s
only limited amount of possible cheap proxies in existence for each thread ‒ if more are
created, it falls back to equivalent of [ load_full](https://docs.rs#method.load_full) internally.

This is therefore a good choice to use for eg. searching a data structure or juggling the pointers around a bit, but not as something to store in larger amounts. The rule of thumb is this is suited for local variables on stack, but not in long-living data structures.

[§](https://docs.rs#consistency)Consistency

In case multiple related operations are to be done on the loaded value, it is generally
recommended to call `load` just once and keep the result over calling it multiple times.
First, keeping it is usually faster. But more importantly, the value can change between the
calls to load, returning different objects, which could lead to logical inconsistency.
Keeping the result makes sure the same object is used.

```
struct Point {
    x: usize,
    y: usize,
}
fn print_broken(p: &ArcSwap<Point>) {
    // This is broken, because the x and y may come from different points,
    // combining into an invalid point that never existed.
    println!("X: {}", p.load().x);
    // If someone changes the content now, between these two loads, we
    // have a problem
    println!("Y: {}", p.load().y);
}
fn print_correct(p: &ArcSwap<Point>) {
    // Here we take a snapshot of one specific point so both x and y come
    // from the same one.
    let point = p.load();
    println!("X: {}", point.x);
    println!("Y: {}", point.y);
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arc_swap/lib.rs.html#514-521)#### pub fn [compare_and_swap](https://docs.rs#method.compare_and_swap)<C>(&self, current: C, new: T) -> [Guard](https://docs.rs/struct.Guard.html)<T, S>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arc_swap/lib.rs.html#514-521)

#### pub fn [compare_and_swap](https://docs.rs#method.compare_and_swap)<C>(&self, current: C, new: T) -> [Guard](https://docs.rs/struct.Guard.html)<T, S>

Swaps the stored Arc if it equals to `current`.

If the current value of the `ArcSwapAny` equals to `current`, the `new` is stored inside.
If not, nothing happens.

The previous value (no matter if the swap happened or not) is returned. Therefore, if the
returned value is equal to `current`, the swap happened. You want to do a pointer-based
comparison to determine it.

In other words, if the caller „guesses“ the value of current correctly, it acts like
[ swap](https://docs.rs#method.swap), otherwise it acts like

[(including the limitations).](https://docs.rs#method.load_full)

`load_full`The `current` can be specified as `&Arc`, [ Guard](https://docs.rs/struct.Guard.html),

[or as a raw pointer (but](https://docs.rs/struct.Guards.html)

`&Guards`*not*owned

`Arc`). See the
[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.AsRaw.html)

`AsRaw`Read-Copy-Update of the pointer inside.

This is useful in read-heavy situations with several threads that sometimes update the data
pointed to. The readers can just repeatedly use [ load](https://docs.rs#method.load) without any locking.
The writer uses this method to perform the update.

In case there’s only one thread that does updates or in case the next version is
independent of the previous one, simple [ swap](https://docs.rs#method.swap) or

[is enough. Otherwise, it may be needed to retry the update operation if some other thread made an update in between. This is what this method does.](https://docs.rs#method.store)

`store`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

This will *not* work as expected, because between loading and storing, some other thread
might have updated the value.

```
let cnt = ArcSwap::from_pointee(0);
thread::scope(|scope| {
    for _ in 0..10 {
        scope.spawn(|_| {
           let inner = cnt.load_full();
            // Another thread might have stored some other number than what we have
            // between the load and store.
            cnt.store(Arc::new(*inner + 1));
        });
    }
}).unwrap();
// This will likely fail:
// assert_eq!(10, *cnt.load_full());
```
This will, but it can call the closure multiple times to retry:

```
let cnt = ArcSwap::from_pointee(0);
thread::scope(|scope| {
    for _ in 0..10 {
        scope.spawn(|_| cnt.rcu(|inner| **inner + 1));
    }
}).unwrap();
assert_eq!(10, *cnt.load_full());
```
Due to the retries, you might want to perform all the expensive operations *before* the
rcu. As an example, if there’s a cache of some computations as a map, and the map is cheap
to clone but the computations are not, you could do something like this:

```
fn expensive_computation(x: usize) -> usize {
    x * 2 // Let's pretend multiplication is *really expensive expensive*
}
type Cache = HashMap<usize, usize>;
static CACHE: Lazy<ArcSwap<Cache>> = Lazy::new(|| ArcSwap::default());
fn cached_computation(x: usize) -> usize {
    let cache = CACHE.load();
    if let Some(result) = cache.get(&x) {
        return *result;
    }
    // Not in cache. Compute and store.
    // The expensive computation goes outside, so it is not retried.
    let result = expensive_computation(x);
    CACHE.rcu(|cache| {
        // The cheaper clone of the cache can be retried if need be.
        let mut cache = HashMap::clone(&cache);
        cache.insert(x, result);
        cache
    });
    result
}
assert_eq!(42, cached_computation(21));
assert_eq!(42, cached_computation(21));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-cost-of-cloning)The cost of cloning

Depending on the size of cache above, the cloning might not be as cheap. You can however
use persistent data structures ‒ each modification creates a new data structure, but it
shares most of the data with the old one (which is usually accomplished by using `Arc`s
inside to share the unchanged values). Something like
[ rpds](https://crates.io/crates/rpds) or

[might do what you need.](https://crates.io/crates/im)

`im`Provides an access to an up to date projection of the carried data.

[§](https://docs.rs#motivation)Motivation

Sometimes, an application consists of components. Each component has its own configuration structure. The whole configuration contains all the smaller config parts.

For the sake of separation and abstraction, it is not desirable to pass the whole configuration to each of the components. This allows the component to take only access to its own part.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetimes--flexibility)Lifetimes & flexibility

This method is not the most flexible way, as the returned type borrows into the `ArcSwap`.
To provide access into eg. `Arc<ArcSwap<T>>`, you can create the [ Map](https://docs.rs/access/struct.Map.html) type directly. See
the

[module.](https://docs.rs/access/index.html)

`access`[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

As the provided function is called on each load from the shared storage, it should generally be cheap. It is expected this will usually be just referencing of a field inside the structure.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use std::sync::Arc;
use arc_swap::ArcSwap;
use arc_swap::access::Access;
struct Cfg {
    value: usize,
}
fn print_many_times<V: Access<usize>>(value: V) {
    for _ in 0..25 {
        let value = value.load();
        println!("{}", *value);
    }
}
let shared = ArcSwap::from_pointee(Cfg { value: 0 });
let mapped = shared.map(|c: &Cfg| &c.value);
crossbeam_utils::thread::scope(|s| {
    // Will print some zeroes and some twos
    s.spawn(|_| print_many_times(mapped));
    s.spawn(|_| shared.store(Arc::new(Cfg { value: 2 })));
}).expect("Something panicked in a thread");
```

# Strategy in arc_swap::strategy - Rust

`pub trait Strategy<T: `[RefCnt](https://docs.rs/trait.RefCnt.html)>: InnerStrategy<T> { }## Expand description

A strategy for protecting the reference counted pointer `T`.

This chooses the algorithm for how the reference counts are protected. Note that the user of the crate can’t implement the trait and can’t access any method; this is hopefully temporary measure to make sure the interface is not part of the stability guarantees of the crate. Once enough experience is gained with implementing various strategies, it will be un-sealed and users will be able to provide their own implementation.

For now, the trait works only as a bound to talk about the types that represent strategies.

# arc_swap::strategy - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arc-swap/1.9.2/arc_swap/strategy/index.html

## Expand description

Strategies for protecting the reference counts.

There are multiple algorithms how to protect the reference counts while they’re being updated
by multiple threads, each with its own set of pros and cons. The [ DefaultStrategy](https://docs.rs/type.DefaultStrategy.html) is used by
default and should generally be the least surprising option. It is possible to pick a different
strategy.

For now, the traits in here are sealed and don’t expose any methods to the users of the crate. This is because we are not confident about the details just yet. In the future it may be possible for downstream users to implement their own, but for now it is only so users can choose one of the provided.

It is expected that future strategies would come with different capabilities and limitations. In particular, some that are not “tight” in the cleanup (delay the cleanup) or not support the compare and swap operations.

Currently, we have these strategies:

- `DefaultStrategy`
- `RwLock<()>`

[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

Formally, the [ RwLock<()>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/rwlock/struct.RwLock.html) may be used as a strategy too. It doesn’t have
the performance characteristics or lock-free guarantees of the others, but it is much simpler
and contains less

`unsafe` code (actually, less code altogether). Therefore, it can be used for
testing purposes and cross-checking.Note that generally, using [ RwLock<Arc<T>>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/rwlock/struct.RwLock.html) is likely to be better
performance wise. So if the goal is to not use third-party unsafe code, only the one in

[, that is the better option. This is provided mostly for investigation and testing of](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/index.html)

`std`[itself or algorithms written to use](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwap.html)

`ArcSwap`[.](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwap.html)

`ArcSwap`*This is not meant to be used in production code*.

- [CaS](https://docs.rs/trait.CaS.html)
- An extension of the `Strategy`

- A strategy for protecting the reference counted pointer `T`.

# RefCnt in arc_swap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arc-swap/1.9.2/arc_swap/trait.RefCnt.html

`pub unsafe trait RefCnt: `[Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) {
    type [Base](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Base);
    // Required methods
    fn [into_ptr](https://docs.rs#tymethod.into_ptr)(me: Self) -> [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)Self::[Base](https://docs.rs/trait.RefCnt.html#associatedtype.Base);
[as_ptr](https://docs.rs#tymethod.as_ptr)(me: &Self) -> [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)Self::[Base](https://docs.rs/trait.RefCnt.html#associatedtype.Base);
[from_ptr](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_ptr)(ptr: [*const ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)Self::[Base](https://docs.rs/trait.RefCnt.html#associatedtype.Base)) -> Self;

[dec](https://docs.rs#method.dec)(ptr: [*const ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)Self::[Base](https://docs.rs/trait.RefCnt.html#associatedtype.Base)) { ... }
}## Expand description

A trait describing smart reference counted pointers.

Note that in a way [ Option<Arc<T>>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html) is also a smart reference counted pointer, just
one that can hold NULL.

The trait is unsafe, because a wrong implementation will break the [ArcSwapAny](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html)
implementation and lead to UB.

This is not actually expected for downstream crate to implement, this is just means to reuse
code for [Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html) and [ Option<Arc>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html) variants. However, it is theoretically possible (if
you have your own

[Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)implementation).

It is also implemented for [Rc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/rc/struct.Rc.html), but that is not considered very useful (because the
[ArcSwapAny](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html) is not `Send` or `Sync`, therefore there’s very little advantage for it to be
atomic).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Aside from the obvious properties (like that incrementing and decrementing a reference count
cancel each out and that having less references tracked than how many things actually point to
the value is fine as long as the count doesn’t drop to 0), it also must satisfy that if two
pointers have the same value, they point to the same object. This is specifically not true for
ZSTs, but it is true for `Arc`s of ZSTs, because they have the reference counts just after the
value. It would be fine to point to a type-erased version of the same object, though (if one
could use this trait with unsized types in the first place).

Methods in this trait must not panic nor unwind.

Furthermore, the type should be Pin (eg. if the type is cloned or moved, it should still point/deref to the same place in memory).

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Provides a view into the smart pointer as a raw pointer.

This must not affect the reference count ‒ the pointer is only borrowed.

Converts a raw pointer back into the smart pointer, without affecting the reference count.

This is only called on values previously returned by [ into_ptr](https://docs.rs#method.into_ptr).
However, it is not guaranteed to be 1:1 relation ‒

`from_ptr` may be called more times than
`into_ptr` temporarily provided the reference count never drops under 1 during that time
(the implementation sometimes owes a reference). These extra pointers will either be
converted back using `into_ptr` or forgotten.[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

This must not be called by code outside of this crate.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Increments the reference count by one.

Return the pointer to the inner thing as a side effect.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# arc_swap::docs::limitations - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arc-swap/1.9.2/arc_swap/docs/limitations/index.html

## Expand description

Limitations and common pitfalls.

[§](https://docs.rs#sized-types)Sized types

This currently works only for `Sized` types. Unsized types have „fat pointers“, which are twice
as large as the normal ones. The [ AtomicPtr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/sync/atomic/type.AtomicPtr.html) doesn’t support them. One could use something
like

`AtomicU128` for them. The catch is this doesn’t exist and the difference would make it
really hard to implement the debt storage/stripped down hazard pointers.A workaround is to use double indirection:

```
// This doesn't work:
// let data: ArcSwap<[u8]> = ArcSwap::new(Arc::from([1, 2, 3]));
// But this does:
let data: ArcSwap<Box<[u8]>> = ArcSwap::from_pointee(Box::new([1, 2, 3]));
```
It also may be possible to use `ArcSwap` with the [ triomphe::ThinArc](https://docs.rs/triomphe/latest/triomphe/struct.ThinArc.html) (that crate needs
enabling a feature flag to cooperate with

`ArcSwap`).There’s only limited number of “fast” slots for borrowing from [ ArcSwap](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwap.html) for each single
thread (currently 8, but this might change in future versions). If these run out, the algorithm
falls back to slower path.

If too many [ Guard](https://docs.rs/struct.Guard.html)s are kept around, the performance might be poor. These are not intended
to be stored in data structures or used across async yield points.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-clone-implementation)No `Clone` implementation

Previous version implemented [ Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html), but it turned out to be very confusing to people, since
it created fully independent

[. Users expected the instances to be tied to each other, that store in one would change the result of future load of the other.](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwap.html)

`ArcSwap`To emulate the original behaviour, one can do something like this:

`let new = ArcSwap::new(old.load_full());`

# arc_swap::docs::performance - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arc-swap/1.9.2/arc_swap/docs/performance/index.html

## Expand description

Performance characteristics.

There are several performance advantages of [ ArcSwap](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwap.html) over

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/rwlock/struct.RwLock.html)

`RwLock`[§](https://docs.rs#lock-free-readers)Lock-free readers

All the read operations are always [lock-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-blocking_algorithm#Lock-freedom). Most of the time, they are actually
[wait-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-blocking_algorithm#Wait-freedom). They may wait from time to time, with at least `usize::MAX / 4` [wait-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-blocking_algorithm#Wait-freedom)
accesses in between waits.

Writers are [lock-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-blocking_algorithm#Lock-freedom).

Whenever the documentation talks about *contention* in the context of [ ArcSwap](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwap.html), it talks
about contention on the CPU level ‒ multiple cores having to deal with accessing the same cache
line. This slows things down (compared to each one accessing its own cache line), but an
eventual progress is still guaranteed and the cost is significantly lower than parking threads
as with mutex-style contention.

[§](https://docs.rs#speeds)Speeds

The base line speed of read operations is similar to using an *uncontended* [ Mutex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/mutex/struct.Mutex.html).
However,

[suffers no contention from any other read operations and only slight ones during updates. The](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.load)

`load`[operation is additionally contended only on the reference count of the](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.load_full)

`load_full`[inside ‒ so, in general, while](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)

`Arc`[rapidly loses its performance when being in active use by multiple threads at once and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/mutex/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`[is slow to start with,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/rwlock/struct.RwLock.html)

`RwLock`[mostly keeps its performance even when read by many threads in parallel.](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwap.html)

`ArcSwap`Write operations are considered expensive. A write operation is more expensive than access to
an *uncontended* [ Mutex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/mutex/struct.Mutex.html) and on some architectures even slower than uncontended

[. However, it is faster than either under contention.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/sync/poison/rwlock/struct.RwLock.html)

`RwLock`There are some (very unscientific) [benchmarks](https://github.com/vorner/arc-swap/tree/master/benches) within the source code of the library, and the
[ DefaultStrategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/type.DefaultStrategy.html) has some numbers measured on my computer.

The exact numbers are highly dependent on the machine used (both absolute numbers and relative between different data structures). Not only architectures have a huge impact (eg. x86 vs ARM), but even AMD vs. Intel or two different Intel processors. Therefore, if what matters is more the speed than the wait-free guarantees, you’re advised to do your own measurements.

Further speed improvements may be gained by the use of the [ Cache](https://docs.rs/cache/struct.Cache.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#consistency)Consistency

The combination of [wait-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-blocking_algorithm#Wait-freedom) guarantees of readers and no contention between concurrent
[ load](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.load)s provides

*consistent*performance characteristics of the synchronization mechanism. This might be important for soft-realtime applications (the CPU-level contention caused by a recent update/write operation might be problematic for some hard-realtime cases, though).

[§](https://docs.rs#choosing-the-right-reading-operation)Choosing the right reading operation

There are several load operations available. While the general go-to one should be
[ load](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.load), there may be situations in which the others are a better match.

The [ load](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.load) usually only borrows the instance from the shared

[. This makes it faster, because different threads don’t contend on the reference count. There are two situations when this borrow isn’t possible. If the content gets changed, all existing](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwap.html)

`ArcSwap`[s are promoted to contain an owned instance. The promotion is done by the writer, but the readers still need to decrement the reference counts of the old instance when they no longer use it, contending on the count.](https://docs.rs/struct.Guard.html)

`Guard`The other situation derives from internal implementation. The number of borrows each thread can
have at each time (across all [ Guard](https://docs.rs/struct.Guard.html)s) is limited. If this limit is exceeded, an owned
instance is created instead.

Therefore, if you intend to hold onto the loaded value for extended time span, you may prefer
[ load_full](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.load_full). It loads the pointer instance (

[) without borrowing, which is slower (because of the possible contention on the reference count), but doesn’t consume one of the borrow slots, which will make it more likely for following](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)

`Arc`[s to have a slot available. Similarly, if some API needs an owned](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.load)

`load``Arc`, [is more convenient and potentially faster then first](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.load_full)

`load_full`[ing and then cloning that](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.load)

`load`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)

`Arc`Additionally, it is possible to use a [ Cache](https://docs.rs/cache/struct.Cache.html) to get further speed improvement at the
cost of less comfortable API and possibly keeping the older values alive for longer than
necessary.

# DefaultStrategy in arc_swap::strategy - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arc-swap/1.9.2/arc_swap/strategy/type.DefaultStrategy.html

`pub type DefaultStrategy = HybridStrategy<DefaultConfig>;`## Expand description

The default strategy.

It is used by the type aliases [ ArcSwap](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwap.html) and

[. Only the other strategies need to be used explicitly.](https://docs.rs/type.ArcSwapOption.html)

`ArcSwapOption`[§](https://docs.rs#performance-characteristics)Performance characteristics

- It is optimized for read-heavy situations, with possibly many concurrent read accesses from multiple threads. Readers don’t contend each other at all.
- Readers are wait-free (with the exception of at most once in `usize::MAX / 4`accesses, which is only lock-free).
- Writers are lock-free.
- Reclamation is exact ‒ the resource is released as soon as possible (works like RAII, not
like a traditional garbage collector; can contain non-`'static`data).

Each thread has a limited number of fast slots (currently 8, but the exact number is not
guaranteed). If it holds at most that many [ Guard](https://docs.rs/struct.Guard.html)s at once, acquiring them is fast. Once
these slots are used up (by holding to these many

[s), acquiring more of them will be slightly slower, but still wait-free.](https://docs.rs/struct.Guard.html)

`Guard`If you expect to hold a lot of “handles” to the data around, or hold onto it for a long time,
you may want to prefer the [ load_full](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.load_full) method.

The speed of the fast slots is in the ballpark of locking an *uncontented* mutex. The advantage
over the mutex is the stability of speed in the face of contention from other threads ‒ while
the performance of mutex goes rapidly down, the slowdown of running out of held slots or heavy
concurrent writer thread in the area of single-digit multiples.

The ballpark benchmark figures (my older computer) are around these, but you’re welcome to run the benchmarks in the git repository or write your own.

- Load (both uncontented and contented by other loads): ~30ns
- `load_full`: ~50ns uncontented, goes up a bit with other- `load_full`in other threads on the same- `Arc`value (~80-100ns).
- Loads after running out of the slots ‒ about 10-20ns slower than `load_full`.
- Stores: Dependent on number of threads, but generally low microseconds.
- Loads with heavy concurrent writer (to the same `ArcSwap`): ~250ns.

# AsRaw in arc_swap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arc-swap/1.9.2/arc_swap/trait.AsRaw.html

## Expand description

A trait describing things that can be turned into a raw pointer.

This is just an abstraction of things that can be passed to the
[ compare_and_swap](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcSwapAny.html#method.compare_and_swap).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::ptr;
use std::sync::Arc;
use arc_swap::ArcSwapOption;
let a = Arc::new(42);
let shared = ArcSwapOption::from(Some(Arc::clone(&a)));
shared.compare_and_swap(&a, Some(Arc::clone(&a)));
shared.compare_and_swap(&None::<Arc<_>>, Some(Arc::clone(&a)));
shared.compare_and_swap(shared.load(), Some(Arc::clone(&a)));
shared.compare_and_swap(&shared.load(), Some(Arc::clone(&a)));
shared.compare_and_swap(ptr::null(), Some(Arc::clone(&a)));
```
Due to technical limitation, this is not implemented for owned `Arc`/`Option<Arc<_>>`, they
need to be borrowed.
